title: The EVOLUTION of the EYE 👁️
description:
The eye didn’t appear fully formed. It evolved. In this video, we trace the evolution of the eye from light-sensing eyespot cells in microbes to ocelli in planarians, to compound eyes in insects, and the camera-type eyes of vertebrates. We unpack Darwin’s often-misquoted passage and show how step-by-step natural selection and intermediate forms make complex vision inevitable. 

Meet pax-6, the master control gene behind eye formation across species, and see why convergent evolution gave cephalopods a sharper wiring while our own retina runs “backwards,” creating a blind spot that no intelligent designer would brag about. 

Along the way we visit the Cambrian and Burgess Shale, learn from blind cavefish (Mexican tetra) and the blind mole rat how evolution also removes organs, and explore pseudogenes and olfactory-receptor losses in primates that traded smell for trichromatic vision. Then we compare our eyesight with champions: the mantis shrimp with 12–16 receptors and polarization vision, tarsiers with night-adapted saucer eyes, scallops that focus images with mirror cups, dragonflies with near-360° motion vision, and bees reading UV nectar guides. 

If you’ve searched for Darwin eye quote explained, pax-6 gene, camera vs compound eye, blind spot design flaw, or why cephalopod eyes lack a blind spot, this is your clear, evidence-based walkthrough of how vision really evolved.

transcript: The eye, a window to the world, a marvel of nature, a masterpiece of evolution. But did you know that the eyes journey is a tale of adaptation, mutation, and surprising transformations? Let us unravel the story of how eyes evolved and how they still carry the scars and relics of our evolutionary past. The structural complexity of the eye is mind-blowing. But even more intricate is the brain that processes the images that we see. If the brain could evolve through natural selection, why not the eye? Not just the eye, but every organ in the body is the result of evolution. Not only humans, but all living beings seen today, as well as those that have become extinct have emerged through evolution. The argument of those who oppose evolution is this. An organ can as sophisticated as the eye cannot evolve through evolution. There is a divine power behind such creation which created all the living and non-living things we see today. In fact, they even quote Charles Darin writing these words in his book the origin of species. Theus loved to quote Charles Darin out of context to make it seem like he doubted the very theory that he was proposing. In simple terms, Darwin was telling that yes, at first glance it might seem absurd to think that something as indicated as the eye could evolve step by step through natural selection. But then he quickly follows up by explaining that if we can find examples of simple ice, slightly more complex eyes and even more advanced eyes in different living species and if each stage provided some sort of advantage to the organism, then the idea of a complex eye evolving through numerous small changes isn't observed at all. It is actually quite logical. So rather than disproving his own theory, Darin was actually laying out the perfect argument for how something as complex as the eye could evolve step by step. This kind of rhetorical setup posing a question and then systematically answering it is a common strategy in scientific writing and Darin was a master of it. So let us see if Darin was right. Do we have evidence of the stepbystep evolution of I still living in our midst? Let's find [Music] out. Life on Earth began around 4 billion years ago. And the first traces of ice, they began to emerge during the Cambrian period around 545 million years ago. Before this, most life was softbodied, making fossil evidence difficult. But what little we find shows that even then, light sensitive cells, the primitive signs of ice existed. Take uglina, a single-sellled organism that still swims in ponds today. It has a light sensitive ice spot, a primitive structure that helps it move toward or away from light. This is where it all began with simple cells detecting light. With its eyes, Ugleina can detect whether there is a light or a shadow. The shadow could be that of a predator. With this primitive advantage, it can escape from its predator better than any organism that did not have this feature. An evolutionary advantage. Next, let us see the eyes of the plenarian flatworms. What helps these organisms is that their eyes are in a kind of a socket. Plenarians have two eyelike structures called oeli which are simple eye spots within a small socket. These oseli are not eyes in the sense that they can form images like our own eyes but they are light sensitive structures that can detect the presence and direction of light. This helps them not only to escape from predators but also to find food easily. To really understand how evolutionary advantage works, let us look at the other end of the spectrum. Let us look at another fascinating example. The blind mole rat. This rodent spends most of its life borrowing underground. Over generations, its ancestors lost the need for functional eyes. Today, its eyes are vestigial, covered by a layer of skin. If you peel back that skin, the eyes are still there, a ghostly reminder of what once was. Another incredible example is the Mexican tetra or blind caveish. Living in the dark underwater caves, these fish have lost their eyesight over millennia. Their eye sockets are now just patches of skin. Yet the genes responsible for eye development are still present in their DNA. It is just that it is deactivated. This shows that evolution don't just create new features. It also takes away features that are no longer necessary. But the story doesn't end here. Meet Paxix, the master control gene for eye development. From fruit flies to humans, Paxix is a gene responsible for the formation of eyes. Both vertebbrates and invertebrates have this master control gene for eye formation. If a mutation occurs in the fruit flies packs gene, it will have no eyes. In humans, a mutation in this gene can cause the Irish to shrink or even disappear. If cambrain organisms had eyes, it means that this gene was functioning in them too. However, the paxis gene existed even before these organisms. It is present in a Chinese wormlike creature that swam in the Venian seas 600 million years ago. This creature was a common ancestor of both vertebbrates and invertebrates. The paxis gene was passed on to both these groups from that common ancestor. Vertebbrates have been around for 530 million years and since that time specialized eyes began to form. Camera type eyes in vertebbrates and comboned eyes in invertebrates. Vertebrates including fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals including us have camera type eyes. In our eyes, light enters through the lens and falls on the retina where visual pigments in photo receptors respond to light. These three pigments enable us to perceive color which is why we have what we call a tri chromatic vision. You can understand more from this video that I have done on how we perceive the colors. Now the greatest example of why the eye was not designed is present in the design itself. Suppose you have a lens and a set of photo receptors to capture light. If you were a designer, which direction would you align the photo receptors? Towards the light source so as to capture the maximum light, right? Well, open your eyes. Our photo receptors are looking in the opposite direction. Incoming light must pass through several layers of cells and nerve fibers before reaching the photo receptors. This can scatter and distort the light reducing image clarity. The point where the optic nerve exits the eye creates a natural blind spot because there are no photo receptors in that area. Our brain fills in this missing information but is still a flaw in design. Which stupid designer would make something like that? Interestingly, sephalopods like octopuses have eyes that are structurally similar to ours but don't have the same backward design. Their photo receptors are positioned directly in front facing the incoming light. This eliminates the blind spot and allows for a more efficient light pathway. This difference in design is a powerful example of convergent evolution where two different evolutionary paths arrive at similar solutions through different routes. So far we have seen examples of simple ice, no ice, looked at our own eyes and seen its highs and lows. Now let us see some examples of eyes that are better than ours. Take the example of the mantis shrimp. They have the most complex eyes in the animal kingdom, capable of detecting 12 to 16 types of color receptors and they can also see polarized light and ultraviolet light. They actually have trinocular vision in each eye, meaning they can gauge depth with just one eye. Meet tarsus. These tiny primates have the largest eyes relative to body size of any mammal. Their eyes are so large that they cannot move them in their sockets, but they can rotate their heads almost 180° like owls. Their large eyes are adapted for night vision, allowing them to spot insects and other prey in low light. Take a look at scallops. They have up to 200 tiny eyes lining the edge of their shell. These eyes contain concave mirrors, not lenses, which reflect light to focus an image on a double- layered retina. Next are our common dragon flies. Their eyes cover most of their head, giving them a nearly 360° field of vision. Each eye is made up of 30,000 individual lenses, making them extremely sensitive to motion. Bees have tricomatic vision. But unlike humans who see red, green and blue, bees see ultraviolet blue and green. Many flowers have ultraviolet patterns known as nectar guides that you and I can't see but stand out vividly to bees. If a so-called perfect creator designed humans and all living beings, wouldn't you expect him to have an eye for detail? Especially when it comes to, well, eyes. Instead, what do we get? A backwards retina, blind spots, and eyes that are far from perfect. Makes you wonder, was the Almighty looking the other way while handing out good vision? So to sum up, there is clear evidence of the evolution of the ice all over the animal kingdom. You can deny it, but that would be to close your eyes on the evidence that are right in front of your own eyes. Remember what Darin said, if we can find those intermediate forms and if each step is useful to the organism, then the evolution of the eye is not only possible but inevitable. I think you have seen it today with your own eyes in this video. Right? If you found this journey through the eyeopening story of evolution insightful, don't just keep it to yourself. Share it with someone who might still be in the dark about how complex structures like the eye came to be. Let us shine a light on science one video at a time. If you like this video, you will love this entire playlist on evolution that I have made. Also a big shout out to all the people who support this channel by having become its members.
